Series::clamp_min¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::clamp_min(double min) const -> Series
Series& Series::clamp_min_(double min)
Series::clamp_min(const Series& min) const -> Series
Series& Series::clamp_min_(const Series& min)

What It Does¶

Floors every element from below: out[i] = self[i] >= min ? self[i] : min — the mirror image of clamp_max. The _ suffix pair mutate self in place instead of returning a new Series.

Parameters¶

min (double or const Series&)

The lower bound. For the double overload, every element is floored at the same value. For the Series overload, the bound broadcasts elementwise against self.

Returns¶

Series (or Series& for the _ variants) A new Series (or self, mutated) with every element >= min.

Gradient¶

Both overloads are differentiable. d(out)/d(self[i]) = 1 where self[i] >= min, else 0 — an inclusive boundary, matching clamp_max’s own convention and, through it, maximum/minimum’s tie-breaking rule. For the Series overload, min gets the complementary gradient: 1 exactly where self[i] < min (see Example 4).

The in-place _ variant is not independently differentiable, for the same reason as clamp_max_: in-place ops in this engine are treated as low-level storage mutations. Use the out-of-place clamp_min() inside anything that needs to backpropagate through the clamp itself.

Examples¶

Example 1. Floor a mix of negative, zero, and positive values at 0.0.

auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{-2.0, -0.5, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0}, {5});
std::cout << x.clamp_min(0.0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0, 1, 3]

Everything at or below 0.0 is raised to the floor; 1.0 and 3.0 already clear it and pass through unchanged. This is exactly how relu() is defined in this engine (relu(x) == clamp_min(x, 0.0)).

Example 2. Gradient at the boundary.

auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{-2.0, -0.5, 0.0, 1.0, 3.0}, {5});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.clamp_min(0.0);
y.sum().reverse();
std::cout << "y=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0, 1, 3]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 1, 1, 1]

x == 0.0 (index 2) gets gradient 1, not 0 — the inclusive boundary.

Example 3. The Series-argument overload: each element is floored at its own, independent bound.

auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{1, 5, 3}, {3});
auto lo = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{2, 2, 2}, {3});
std::cout << x.clamp_min(lo);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 5, 3]

1 is below its bound of 2, so it’s raised to 2; 5 and 3 already clear their bound and pass through unchanged.

Example 4. Gradient of the Series-argument overload: it flows to self where self was kept, and to min where the bound was used instead.

auto x = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{1, 5, 3}, {3});
auto lo = pluss::make_series(std::vector<double>{2, 2, 2}, {3});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
lo.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.clamp_min(lo);
y.sum().reverse();
std::cout << "y=" << y << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "dlo=" << lo.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 5, 3]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 1]
dlo=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0, 0]

Index 0 (x=1 < lo=2, the bound was used): gradient goes to lo. Indices 1 and 2 (x >= lo, x passed through): gradient goes to x instead — the mirror image of clamp_max’s Example 4.

Notes¶

  • clamp_min(x, 0.0) is literally how relu(x) is defined in this engine.

  • clamp_min’s inclusive boundary at self[i] == min mirrors clamp_max’s own — see its Gradient section for why that boundary choice matters.

See Also¶

  • Series::clamp_max: the mirrored ceiling.

  • Series::maximum: semantically equivalent to the Series-argument overload (self.clamp_min(lo) == self.maximum(lo)), though implemented separately via where() rather than sharing code with it.
